etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English perishen, borrowed from Old French perir (via the stem periss- used in various conjugations), from Latin perīre (“pass away, perish”), from per (“through”) + īre (“pass, go”).

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To decay and disappear; to waste away to nothing.

quote.citation: 1881, Tarafa, translated by W. A. Clouston, The Poem of Tarafa
quote.text: I consider time as a treasure decreasing every night; and that which every day diminishes soon perishes for ever.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To decay in such a way that it cannot be used for its original purpose

quote.citation: 2015, Christopher Cumo, Foods that Changed History:
quote.text: The difficulty is that fresh foods perish due to the multiplication in them of harmful bacteria.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To die; to cease to live.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Proverbs 11:10:
quote.text: When it goeth well with the righteous, the citie reioyceth: and when the wicked perish, there is shouting.

quote.citation: 1719 May 6 (Gregorian calendar), [Daniel Defoe], The Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe, […], London:  […]  W[illiam] Taylor […], →OCLC:
quote.text: […] the ship struck upon a sand, and  […]  the sea broke over her in such a manner that we expected we should all have perished immediately; and we were immediately driven into our close quarters, to shelter us from the very foam and spray of the sea.

quote.citation: 1625, Francis [Bacon], “Of Friendship”, in The Essayes […], 3rd edition, London:  […]  Iohn Haviland for Hanna Barret, →OCLC:
quote.text: that closeness did impair and a little perish his understanding

quote.citation: 1898, William Pett Ridge, By Order of the Magistrate, page 209:
